706a5c1e1cd86345: PETALING JAYA: The death of a 31-year-old man from Kubang Pasu has been confirmed to be the first human rabies case in Kedah since 1998.
The state health department (JKN) said the man who died today had been bitten by a stray dog in August, Bernama reported.
It said the victim sought treatment at a healthcare facility after the incident but did not receive rabies post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP).

“On Sept 18, the victim began experiencing fatigue, weakness and numbness in the right upper limb. The symptoms progressed to difficulty swallowing, hydrophobia, aerophobia, anxiety and behavioural changes on Sept 22, consistent with the clinical manifestations of rabies.
“The following day, the victim sought treatment again and was referred for further treatment before being admitted to the intensive care unit,” Kedah JKN said in a statement today.
It said clinical samples taken on Sept 24 were confirmed by laboratory tests two days later to be positive for rabies.

“Following the confirmation, Kedah JKN, the Kubang Pasu district health office, the Kedah veterinary services department and relevant agencies implemented control and prevention measures, including active case detection, health education, enhanced surveillance of animal-bite cases, risk assessment and control of stray animals in the affected area.

“As this is the first human rabies case reported in Kedah since 1998, the health ministry, together with Kedah JKN and relevant agencies, is conducting a comprehensive epidemiological investigation to identify the source of infection and route of exposure,” it added.

The investigation includes examining the victim’s travel and exposure history, identifying contacts and risk factors, and analysing the timeline of events to determine the source and factors associated with the infection.

Kedah JKN said control measures were also being strengthened under the "One Health" approach, involving human exposure management, surveillance of animal-bite cases, as well as monitoring and risk assessment of dogs and other potentially exposed animals in high-risk areas.

It said that as of August 2026, a total of 502 animal bite and scratch cases had been reported in Kedah, with 65.3% involving dogs, 23.1% cats and 11.6% other animals, adding that of these, 56.2% involved domestic animals and 43.8% stray animals.

It reminded the public that rabies can be transmitted through bites, scratches or exposure to the saliva of infected animals, and urged pet owners to ensure their dogs and cats receive anti-rabies vaccinations.

Kedah JKN also said that anyone bitten or scratched by an animal should immediately wash the wound with soap and running water for at least 15 minutes and seek medical attention at a public or private healthcare facility for risk assessment and appropriate treatment.
30a425da57f4b278: KUALA LUMPUR: It was business as usual at Universiti Malaya today, a day after flash floods briefly affected parts of the campus following heavy rain.
The floodwaters near the university's main gate receded within hours yesterday, with no further flooding reported today and campus activities continuing as usual.
Checks at the university today found registration for new students and residential college reporting proceeding as scheduled, with parents and family members accompanying their children.
UM's Student Affairs Department had earlier announced that physical registration and reporting for residential college accommodation for new students would begin on Sept 26.
The university is also scheduled to hold its Week of Welcome (UM-WOW) from tomorrow till Oct 2, subject to changes.
The flash floods occurred about 5.15pm yesterday following heavy rain in Kuala Lumpur, with videos shared on social media showing knee-deep water in front of the university campus.
A UM spokesman confirmed that the floodwaters had receded within 30 minutes and the situation on campus had returned to normal.

Checks on social media, however, found comments claiming that the flooding near the university's main entrance was not a new occurrence, with some users alleging that the area had experienced similar flooding for decades, including claims that it had been happening for as long as 30 years.
Law student Tang Yi Ze said the university administration should review the drainage system and take steps to improve it for the welfare of students.
"Since I entered UM, the drain beside the Faculty of Law has consistently filled to dangerously high levels during heavy rain.

"Almost every time it rains, the alarm at the faculty is triggered. Students and staff who drive to the faculty have to move their cars if they are parked near the drain. There are several parking spaces near the drain, although some are located further away.
"Things have not improved over the past three years and the road in front of the Faculty of Law, which is very close to the KL Gate is frequently flooded."
The New Straits Times has reached out to Universiti Malaya for comments on the claims, as well as any measures taken or planned to address the issue.
f96443002bf2cc5b: FAIRFORD: British counter-terrorism police Sunday were reportedly probing a major incident near a base used by the US air force after several men were arrested on suspicion of explosives offences.

Villagers in the nearby village of Whelford had been evacuated and army bomb disposal experts were "currently examining a number of vehicles", police in the southwestern county of Gloucestershire said in a statement.

Several UK media including the BBC and Sky News reported that the counter-terrorism force was leading the investigation into the incident near RAF Fairford, but that was not immediately confirmed to AFP.
A cordon is in place and officers believed the incident had been "contained".
Broadcast aerial footage showed a bomb disposal robot on a rural road moving around two white vans with their rear doors open and a third with its doors closed.
Villager Julian Tudsbury told the BBC another resident alerted police to three "suspicious vans" in the village in the early hours.
In March, then prime minister Keir Starmer granted permission for "defensive" US action against Iranian missile sites from two UK bases including Fairford.
Prime minister Andy Burnham was being kept updated on the incident, a government spokesman said.
"We are grateful to the emergency services, who have acted quickly to detain several suspects and put measures in place to keep the community safe," the spokesman said.
"It would be inappropriate to comment further whilst investigations are ongoing."
Defence minister Wes Streeting thanked "emergency and specialist teams" deployed to the scene.
"We can be reassured that this is being dealt with," he said on X.
Media reported a large emergency services presence in the area including a Hazardous Area Response Team.
"A number of properties are currently being evacuated in the Whelford area following the declaration of a major incident," Gloucestershire Police said.
Several men had been arrested "on suspicion of offences under the Explosives Act", the force added.
Villagers evacuated
"Residents from the nearby village of Whelford had been evacuated to a nearby leisure centre," police said.
Whelford is adjacent to the Royal Air Force Fairford base, which is also used by the US Air Force.
Fairford is the UK base of the 501st Combat Support Wing, a US air force administrative support wing.
It said in a statement that no US air force personnel had been involved in the incident.
"The 501st Combat Support Wing appreciates the swift response and continued support of our local law enforcement partners," it said.
"We remain in close coordination with our UK partners to help ensure the safety and security of both our military and local communities," it added.
The MP for the area, Roz Savage, described the situation as "worrying".
"I have contacted the police for further updates and I’ve been told that it is believed the incident is contained," she said on X.
The incident comes amid concerns about the actions of hostile foreign states.
Interior minister Shabana Mahmood has accused Iran and Russia of using proxies to carry out criminal activities on their behalf on UK territory.
Earlier this month, reports said British military sites were targeted by drones more than 300 times over the past year.

Britain's defence ministry did not disclose who was behind the drone activity, but the figures come as European countries warned of an increase in suspected Russian hybrid operations on their territory.
UK armed forces minister Louise Sandher-Jones told AFP in a statement that the government was "taking the threat posed by hostile drones to defence sites extremely seriously".
38976d21137de794: KUALA LUMPUR: Former federal territories minister Dr Zaliha Mustafa has denied allegations that she had attended, officiated, or been involved in any groundbreaking ceremonies for new settlements for Myanmar refugees.
She emphasised that the allegations circulating on social media are false and malicious, in addition to linking a photograph of her with an individual to something that never happened.
"I do not personally know the individual in question and do not have any relationship or dealings, whether official or unofficial, with him," she said in a Facebook post today.

According to her, the circulated photo is believed to have been taken at the Asean sustainable urbanisation forum, Asean governors and mayors forum, and the meeting of governors and mayors of Asean capitals 2025 in the capital city on Aug 12, 2025.
Zaliha said she was invited to deliver a special address and subsequently attend the launch ceremony for the programme, which was officiated by deputy prime minister Fadillah Yusof.
"The programme is open to the public to register as participants. Therefore, I certainly do not know the identity of every individual who attended.
"A photo with a participant does not mean I know the person, have a relationship with him, invited him personally, or support his views or actions," she said.

The Sekijang MP said she would report the matter to the Malaysian Communications and Multimedia Commission (MCMC) regarding the dissemination of the post for review and appropriate action according to the law.

Meanwhile, Zaliha said the allegation that she supported or facilitated the resettlement of new Myanmar refugees was also inconsistent with the record of actions she took while leading the federal territories department.

She said among the measures implemented was the establishment of the KL Strike Force as an integrated enforcement mechanism to address issues of security and public order, particularly in the capital, including the issue of the influx of foreign nationals and the illegal settlement of Myanmar refugees.
"In fact, the first operation of the KL Strike Force was to raid the illegal settlement of Myanmar refugees in Bandar Baru Sentul.
"Through KL Strike Force, I emphasised that action should be taken against illegal settlements and structures, unlicensed businesses, and foreign activities without proper authorisation," she added.
Therefore, she urged all parties not to take a single photo out of context to build a narrative that is not based on facts.
ba8df0180cee9b52: NAGOYA: An injury mark across her forehead is a daily reminder of a near-fatal crash, but Malaysia's S. Sivasangari seems to have erased that nightmare as she defended her Asian Games title on Sunday — also booking her ticket to the 2028 Los Angeles Games when squash makes its Olympic debut.
The collision near Kuala Lumpur left Sivasangari with neck and spine injuries and raised doubts about whether she would walk again.
Yet within a year or so, she was not just walking but climbing the podium, claiming two Asian Games golds in Hangzhou in a remarkable testament to her willpower and skill.
"I definitely went through a tough journey," the 27-year-old said after blanking India's Anahat Singh 11-4, 11-4, 11-7 in the women's singles final at the Kinjo Futo Arena.
"The car crash was like four years ago and then the Asian Games was a huge comeback.
"I think everything happens for a reason, you know. I believe there's always highs and lows. My low was pretty low, but I'm glad I managed to bounce back.
"Life is full of struggles, so I'm trying to not overthink too much. I try to live life a bit more and not put much pressure on myself and try to enjoy my squash as much as I can."
She refused to let the stakes — victory and Olympic qualification — affect her game.
"I just tried to put that away, all those external factors. I think everyone wants to win it, everyone has the same goal to win the title," she said.
"I try to put that away and just focus on what I need to do on court and I think I managed to do that well and manage my emotions well."
With qualification secured, the world No. 5 has set her sights on twin targets — becoming the world No. 1 and the Olympic champion.
"I want to improve my ranking by the end of the season to be in top three in the world. (Being the) world No. 1 and an Olympic gold medal is my goal," she added.
"I still have two more seasons to play till the Olympics comes. I have a lot more goals, small goals, that I want to achieve before that."
Compatriot Eain Yow Ng also qualified for the LA Games after defending his men's singles title by overpowering Abhay Singh 11-9, 11-5, 11-5 in another Malaysia-India final. - REUTERS
8f8bf196273ac033: The idea was big, exciting, and inspiring: What if we could get every kid in the world access to a computer? For a bunch of thinkers and executives in Silicon Valley, it felt like the way to fix everything. But the One Laptop Per Child initiative, and the XO-1 laptop designed to be given away, were both more complicated than anyone expected.

In the next episode of Version History, David Pierce is joined by The Verge's Adi Robertson and tech journalist David Imel to figure out why OLPC didn't work, whether there's anything to learn from the XO-1's innovative design, and if this kind of computer giveaway could ever succeed.
Read the full story at The Verge.
767f6c4494573d60: KUALA LUMPUR: Negri Sembilan Menteri Besar Datuk Ismail Lasim and several state assemblymen have begun arriving at the Umno headquarters here to attend a meeting on the constitutional crisis in the state.

Among those who arrived were three of the 10 former state executive councillors whose appointments were revoked on Sept 20, namely Sikamat assemblyman Datuk Razali Abu Samah, Chembong assemblyman Datuk Zaifulbahri Idris and Linggi assemblyman Datuk Mohd Faizal Ramli.
Pertang assemblyman Datuk Seri Jalaluddin Alias, who is the Negri Sembilan Umno liaison committee chairman, was also seen arriving at Menara Dato' Onn, World Trade Centre Kuala Lumpur.

Earlier today, Umno president Datuk Seri Dr Ahmad Zahid Hamidi said he would meet all 25 Negri Sembilan assemblymen from Barisan Nasional and Perikatan Nasional tonight to discuss options to resolve the political crisis in the state.
Zahid said the meeting was aimed at coordinating efforts to find a solution to the impasse without interfering in the state administration.
He said the views of the 25 assemblymen would be taken into consideration in determining the options available to resolve the situation.

The Negri Sembilan crisis intensified following the revocation of the appointments of 10 state executive councillors by the Yang di-Pertuan Besar of Negri Sembilan Tuanku Muhriz Tuanku Munawir, which took effect on Sept 20.
The gazette stated that the appointments were revoked after the 10 state executive councillors breached their oath of allegiance to Tuanku Muhriz.
The revocation was made under Article 38(5) of the Negri Sembilan Constitution 1959.
The move came a week after the 10 state executive councillors issued a statement affirming a proclamation seeking to remove Tuanku Muhriz.
However, the Dewan Keadilan dan Undang maintained that the proclamation was invalid under the state Constitution, law and customs.
1df4000fa59dca91: PUTRAJAYA, Sept 27 — Malaysia initially requested that the search and rescue (SAR) operation involving 55 Malaysians who are still uncontactable in Nepal cover the area from Rasuwagadhi to Syabrubesi, but the national team was only allowed to conduct searches in certain areas.

Malaysia Solidarity: Families in Hope (MASFIH) spokesman Dr Manivannan Rethinam said the matter was conveyed to the next of kin during a closed-door meeting with government agencies at Wisma Putra today.

He said the families raised the question of why the Special Malaysia Disaster Assistance and Rescue Team (SMART) operation was not focused on Rasuwagadhi, which is a border area between Nepal and Tibet, believed to be one of the last locations many Malaysians were involved.

According to him, the Chargé d’Affaires ad interim of the Malaysian Embassy in Kathmandu, Mohd Firdaus Azman, explained that Malaysia had requested the Nepalese authorities to extend the search area from Rasuwagadhi to Syabrubesi. However, the permission granted by the Nepalese authorities to the Malaysian team only covers certain areas, including Timure.

“Their (SMART) search area is focused on areas C and D. They cover from Timure to Syabrubesi. That is not the focal area where many Malaysians are missing because we have information on the last known locations and most of them are concentrated in the Rasuwagadhi area, on the Tibet-Nepal border,” he told the media after a nearly four-hour briefing session here today.
Manivannan said the families understand that the SMART operation area is subject to the approval of the Nepalese authorities and that the matter is beyond the team’s control.
He simultaneously expressed appreciation for SMART’s efforts, which also provided explanations to the families about the operations and challenges faced by the team during their time in Nepal.
According to Manivannan, the families also inquired about the possibility of the victims still being found alive.

He said that the SMART commander Senior Fire and Rescue Officer 1 (PgKB 1) Abdul Manaf Che Isa had said that the possibility still exists if there are victims in remote areas or villages in the mountainous region, but the chances are very slim.
“As family members, we still hope for the best. But we also have to move on to the next stage,” he said.

Previously, the SMART Team, consisting of 11 members, was sent to Nepal on September 5 and conducted ground searches and monitoring using drones in areas approved and deemed safe by the Nepalese authorities before returning to Malaysia on September 14.
In addition, Manivannan said the families were informed that Nepal would process the DNA samples from the disaster victims’ bodies to match them with the family’s DNA profiles.
He said the families had previously been informed about the report that Nepal needed assistance to carry out the DNA process due to a lack of expertise.
However, based on today’s briefing, the Nepalese authorities now have sufficient expertise and will carry out the process themselves.

“So far, they are only collecting DNA but it has not been processed yet. Previously, there were media reports in Nepal stating that Nepal needed assistance to process DNA because they lacked expertise. But today, Firdaus from the Malaysian Embassy in Nepal said that Nepal already has enough expertise. They will process it themselves,” he said.
Manivannan said that essentially, the DNA profile obtained from the families will be used for matching with the DNA from the found remains.
According to him, if there is a match, it can help the authorities identify the identity of the body in question.
Commenting on the procedure in the event of a DNA match, Manivannan said based on the explanation received by the families, DNA will be taken from the body before burial.
If a match with family members is later obtained, he said there is a process to retrieve the body to allow the family to conduct a ceremony or bring it home.
However, he emphasised that the families have not yet received official information regarding the entire procedure. — Bernama

fa9e223ba7796d96: ALOR SETAR, Sept 27 — The State Health Department (JKN) of Kedah has reported the state’s first human rabies case since 1998, involving a 31-year-old man from Kubang Pasu who died today after being bitten by a stray dog in August.
It said that the victim sought treatment at a healthcare facility after the incident but did not receive rabies post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP).

“On September 18, the victim began experiencing fatigue, weakness and numbness in the right upper limb. The symptoms progressed to difficulty swallowing, hydrophobia, aerophobia, anxiety and behavioural changes on September 22, consistent with the clinical manifestations of rabies.
“The following day, the victim sought treatment again and was referred for further treatment before being admitted to the Intensive Care Unit (ICU),” it said in a statement today.
It said clinical samples taken on Sept 24 were confirmed by laboratory tests two days later to be positive for rabies.

“Following the confirmation, Kedah JKN, the Kubang Pasu District Health Office, the Kedah Veterinary Services Department and relevant agencies implemented control and prevention measures, including active case detection, health education, enhanced surveillance of animal-bite cases, risk assessment and control of stray animals in the affected area.

“As this is the first human rabies case reported in Kedah since 1998, the Ministry of Health (MOH), together with Kedah JKN and relevant agencies, is conducting a comprehensive epidemiological investigation to identify the source of infection and route of exposure,” it added.

The investigation includes examining the victim’s travel and exposure history, identifying contacts and risk factors, and analysing the timeline of events to determine the source and factors associated with the infection.

Kedah JKN said control measures were also being strengthened under the ‘One Health’ approach, involving human exposure management, surveillance of animal-bite cases and monitoring and risk assessment of dogs and other potentially exposed animals in high-risk areas.

It said that as of August 2026, a total of 502 animal bite and scratch cases had been reported in Kedah, with 65.3 per cent involving dogs, 23.1 per cent cats and 11.6 per cent other animals, adding that of these, 56.2 per cent involved domestic animals and 43.8 per cent stray animals.

It reminded the public that rabies can be transmitted through bites, scratches or exposure to the saliva of infected animals, and urged pet owners to ensure their dogs and cats receive anti-rabies vaccinations.

Kedah JKN also said that anyone bitten or scratched by an animal should immediately wash the wound with soap and running water for at least 15 minutes and seek medical attention at a public or private healthcare facility for risk assessment and appropriate treatment. — Bernama

“Memandangkan kes ini merupakan kes rabies dalam kalangan manusia pertama yang dilaporkan di Kedah sejak 1998, Kementerian Kesihatan (KKM) bersama-sama JKN Kedah dan agensi berkaitan sedang menjalankan siasatan epidemiologi secara menyeluruh bagi mengenal pasti sumber jangkitan dan laluan pendedahan,” menurut kenyataan itu.

“Tindakan kawalan sedang diperkukuh berasaskan pendekatan ‘One Health’ melalui pengesanan dan pengurusan pendedahan manusia, survelan kes gigitan haiwan, pemantauan serta penilaian risiko terhadap anjing dan haiwan yang berpotensi terdedah, serta pelaksanaan tindakan kawalan di kawasan berisiko.

8504108b938c286f: Ada sesuatu yang menarik dalam cara kita melihat perubahan dasar. Rakyat mengeluh, isu mendapat perhatian, pemimpin campur tangan, tindakan diambil dan akhirnya penyelesaian diumumkan.

Pada pandangan pertama, ini tentunya sesuatu yang baik. Pemimpin memang perlu mendengar dan kerajaan yang responsif sepatutnya bersedia membetulkan keadaan apabila sesuatu dasar tidak menghasilkan kesan seperti diharapkan.

Namun ada satu persoalan yang tidak kurang penting: bagaimana jika masalah yang akhirnya diselesaikan itu berkait dengan keputusan kerajaan sendiri atau kelemahan sistem yang sepatutnya mengesannya lebih awal?

Lihat sahaja isu bil elektrik baru-baru ini. Selepas keresahan pengguna mengenai kenaikan bil mendapat perhatian, Perdana Menteri Anwar Ibrahim mengadakan mesyuarat khas pada 17 Sept bersama kementerian dan agensi berkaitan. Kerajaan kemudian memperluas perlindungan bil elektrik bagi pengguna domestik daripada penggunaan 600kWj kepada 800kWj sebulan bagi tempoh September hingga 31 Dis.
Tidak ada yang salah dengan keputusan itu. Malah, kerajaan yang sanggup membuat penyesuaian apabila keadaan berubah menunjukkan dasar tidak semestinya kaku.

Tetapi analisis dasar tidak sepatutnya berhenti pada cerita bahawa pemimpin mendengar lalu masalah selesai. Kita juga perlu bertanya bagaimana masalah itu timbul, apakah andaian asal yang tidak menjadi, apakah kesan yang tidak dijangka dan mengapa pembetulan akhirnya diperlukan.

Isu bekalan Baja Padi 3 di kawasan Lembaga Kemajuan Pertanian Muda (MADA) memberikan satu lagi contoh. Pada 18 Ogos, MADA memaklumkan hanya 22% daripada 616,015 beg baja yang diperlukan sudah dibekalkan, dengan kelewatan itu menjejaskan keperluan kira-kira 38,000 pesawah. Pada 6 Sept, Anwar mengarahkan SPRM menyiasat kelewatan tersebut dan siasatan kemudiannya dibuka.
Sekali lagi, persoalannya bukan sama ada perdana menteri patut campur tangan. Jika masalah menjejaskan rakyat, tentunya pemimpin tertinggi wajar bertindak.
Persoalan yang lebih besar ialah: mengapa sesuatu masalah perlu sampai kepada perdana menteri sebelum sistem benar-benar bergerak?

Kita memerlukan kepimpinan yang responsif, tetapi pada masa sama kita juga memerlukan sistem yang responsif. Pemimpin perlu bertindak apabila sistem terlepas pandang sesuatu masalah, tetapi sistem yang matang tidak sepatutnya bergantung kepada perhatian seorang pemimpin untuk mengesan dan menyelesaikan setiap isu.

Di sinilah kes baja dan bil elektrik bertemu. Kedua-duanya bukan sekadar cerita mengenai pemimpin yang mendengar rakyat. Ia juga mengajak kita melihat apa yang berlaku sebelum masalah mendapat perhatian politik.

Adakah tanda awal sudah kelihatan? Adakah aduan sudah diterima? Adakah data menunjukkan sesuatu tidak berjalan seperti dirancang? Apakah mekanisme pembetulan yang tersedia dan mengapa ia tidak berfungsi lebih awal?

Ukuran sistem yang baik bukanlah berapa banyak masalah akhirnya berjaya diselesaikan selepas campur tangan pemimpin, tetapi berapa banyak masalah dapat dikesan dan diselesaikan sebelum perlu sampai ke peringkat itu.
Bila yang viral dianggap vital
Persoalan ini semakin penting dalam zaman media sosial. Selama ini kita sering bercakap mengenai dasar berasaskan bukti — keputusan dibuat berdasarkan data, penilaian dan pengalaman pelaksanaan.
Namun hari ini muncul satu lagi realiti: dasar yang bergerak selepas sesuatu isu menjadi tular. Aduan tersebar luas, tekanan awam meningkat, perhatian politik datang dan sistem mula bergerak.
Media sosial tentunya boleh menjadi sistem amaran awal yang berguna. Ia membolehkan masalah yang mungkin terlepas daripada radar birokrasi mendapat perhatian pembuat keputusan.
Bahaya timbul apabila sesuatu isu perlu menjadi viral sebelum dianggap vital.

Apa yang tular mengukur perhatian, bukan semestinya kepentingan. Isu kecil boleh menjadi besar kerana naratifnya mudah atau individu berpengaruh membangkitkannya, manakala masalah serius dalam kalangan kelompok yang kurang mempunyai akses kepada media sosial mungkin terus berlaku dalam senyap.
Sebab itu aduan yang kelihatan kecil tidak wajar terus diketepikan sebagai kes terpencil. Ia mungkin petanda awal kepada masalah yang lebih besar.
Cabaran sebenar kerajaan bukan sekadar menunjukkan ia mampu bertindak selepas sesuatu isu tular. Sistem yang baik sepatutnya mampu mengenal pasti apa yang penting sebelum ia terpaksa menjadi tular.
Kredit dan akauntabiliti
Kerajaan juga tidak perlu malu mengubah dasar. Kita terlalu mudah menyifatkan setiap perubahan sebagai pusingan U.
Ada perubahan yang dibuat kerana keadaan berubah. Ada yang berlaku kerana pelaksanaan memberikan maklumat baharu. Ada juga keputusan asal yang memang perlu diperbetulkan.
Kerajaan yang tidak pernah mengubah dasar bukan semestinya kerajaan yang konsisten. Ia juga boleh menjadi kerajaan yang tidak mahu belajar.
Sebab itu apabila sesuatu dasar berubah, soalan yang lebih berguna bukan sekadar “mengapa berubah lagi?”, tetapi apakah yang diketahui hari ini yang tidak diketahui ketika keputusan asal dibuat?
Adakah muncul bukti baharu? Adakah andaian asal tersasar? Adakah keadaan berubah? Atau pelaksanaan menghasilkan kesan yang tidak dijangkakan?
Jika perkara itu diterangkan dengan terbuka, perubahan dasar boleh dilihat sebagai proses pembelajaran.
Namun politik mempunyai logiknya sendiri. Sudah tentu mana-mana pemimpin mahu menunjukkan bahawa mereka mendengar rakyat, bertindak pantas dan mampu menyelesaikan masalah.
Tidak salah memberikan kredit apabila pembetulan dibuat. Tetapi kredit terhadap penyelesaian tidak sepatutnya dipisahkan daripada akauntabiliti terhadap apa yang berlaku sebelumnya.
Jika kerajaan yang sama membuat atau mempertahankan sesuatu keputusan sebelum kemudian memperbetulkannya, kedua-dua bahagian cerita itu perlu disebut.
Jika tidak, kita hanya melihat babak akhirnya — rakyat mengadu, pemimpin datang dan masalah selesai — sedangkan persoalan tentang bagaimana masalah itu berlaku hilang daripada cerita.

Politik mungkin bertanya siapa yang menyelesaikan masalah. Analisis dasar perlu pergi lebih jauh: siapa membuat keputusan, apa yang tidak menjadi, bagaimana kesannya dikesan dan mengapa masalah itu perlu diselesaikan semula.
Pendek kata, kita juga perlu melihat apa yang berlaku sebelum kamera tiba.
Kerajaan tidak perlu takut mengakui sesuatu dasar perlu diperbetulkan. Pembetulan bukan kegagalan jika kerajaan belajar daripadanya.
Tetapi pembetulan juga tidak sepatutnya menjadi jalan mudah untuk memisahkan kredit hari ini daripada akauntabiliti semalam.
Akhirnya, perubahan dasar sepatutnya menjadi bukti bahawa sistem mampu belajar — bukan sekadar peluang untuk pembuat keputusan muncul pada penghujung cerita sebagai pihak yang menyelesaikan masalah.
Penulis ialah profesor di Jabatan Sains Politik dan Pengajian Madani Universiti Islam Antarabangsa Malaysia.

dd9b810fff425b3c: SEPTEMBER 27 — Thirty seconds of dialogue. That’s all it took.
“I’m Tamil. My family’s from Sri Lanka.”
Maitreyi Ramakrishnan, 24, said it as a character in a Netflix comedy about a college dance team. It wasn’t a speech or a protest. It was a throwaway line in a scene nobody would remember.

Within days, Sinhala nationalist Facebook pages were telling their followers to rate Best of the Best one star, with no need to watch it. One page gave out a ready-made prompt so ChatGPT or Gemini could write the abuse for them, then demanded screenshots as proof. The rating fell so sharply that IMDb posted a warning: unusual voting activity.
Read that again. Grown adults were so threatened by a young woman saying her own name that they had a machine write their hatred for them.
That is not patriotism. It is panic.

But not everyone joined the mob. In those same comment threads, some Sinhala-speaking voices pushed back. They said, in effect, leave her alone; judge the film, not the woman. Remember them. This essay is really for them.
Your passport is not your people

Maitreyi’s parents fled Sri Lanka’s civil war with little more than their lives and made a home in Canada. The original script had her character say “Tamil Sri Lankan.” She asked for the change because that is not how she describes herself. Her culture is Tamil, her country is Canada, and her roots are in Sri Lanka. She calls herself an Eelam Tamil.
So let’s be clear about what she actually said.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
The author argues that Sri Lanka can only heal by confronting injustices committed by all sides and building a society where identity no longer determines who is allowed to belong. — File pic

Sri Lankan is a passport. Tamil is the language your grandmother sang to you in, a way of cooking, a way of grieving, a history. Sinhalese is all of that too, in its own language. Saying “I am Tamil” rejects no one. Saying “my country is Canada” declares war on no one. It is someone telling you where she feels at home. The decent response is to listen.
If you want to understand why so many diaspora Tamils won’t say “Sri Lankan,” the answer is brutally simple. Their families fled a country that tried to kill them.
A country cannot demand love from people it taught to be afraid. Belonging can’t be ordered. It has to be earned.
The word that terrifies them is 2,000 years old
Take the word Eelam.

To a nationalist, it sounds like a flag on a battlefield. But the word is older than the war and older than the nation. More than two thousand years ago, Tamil poets of the Sangam age were already writing about Eelam. An ancient inscription carved in Tamil-Brahmi mentions a householder from Eelam. The word has been in our literature longer than most modern countries have existed.
Yes, “Tamil Eelam” came to mean a demand for a separate homeland in the North and East. That is real, and I won’t pretend otherwise. But a heritage is not a manifesto. A name is not a threat.
This fear was built, one law and one fire at a time
The fear did not come from nowhere. It was built, law by law and fire by fire.
1948: months after independence, the new state stripped citizenship from hundreds of thousands of Up-Country Tamils, the people whose hands picked the tea the world still drinks.
1956: the Sinhala Only Act. Overnight, your mother tongue became a barrier to a government job.
The 1970s: university admission rules that told Tamil students their marks counted for less.
1981: the Jaffna Public Library burned. Nearly a hundred thousand books and manuscripts were lost, and with them some of the only surviving records of Tamil memory on this island, in one night.
July 1983: Black July. Tamils were pulled from buses and homes and hunted through the streets of Colombo while the country watched.

Then the war: twenty-six years, an estimated 100,000 dead or more, hundreds of thousands displaced, and a diaspora scattered from Toronto to London to Kuala Lumpur. It ended in 2009 with a final offensive in which, by UN estimates, tens of thousands of civilians may have died, trapped on a thin strip of beach with nowhere left to run.
This is the history carried by Maitreyi’s one line of dialogue.

None of it makes a twenty-year-old Sinhalese student personally guilty. Guilt is not inherited by blood. But every generation inherits a choice: deny the truth or face it, defend the old injustices or make sure they never happen again. Remembrance is necessary. Inherited hatred is poison.
Now the part Tamils won’t want to read
Now I have to turn the mirror around, because an essay that only points one way is just propaganda with better manners.

The LTTE said it fought in our name. It also murdered Tamil politicians and dissenters, took children and handed them guns, and sent suicide bombers into crowded buses and city streets. In 1990, it drove the entire Muslim population out of the North. Tens of thousands of people were given as little as 48 hours to leave homes their families had lived in for generations. That was not a Sinhalese crime. It was ours.
A Tamil who demands accountability from Colombo while staying silent about that has not earned the right to be angry.

And it is not only history. Recently in Jaffna, someone complained to me that lower-caste families were buying land in the neighbourhood. Their relatives abroad had sent money, and now they could afford good homes. Their presence, I was told, was “ruining” the area.

I felt the shame burn in my face. We survived pogroms, and some of us still keep lists of who belongs on our street. A community’s suffering does not make it incapable of injustice. Sometimes it only gives that injustice a better excuse.

So the rule has to be the same for everyone, with no exceptions: no people should have to give up their safety, their rights or their home so that another people can feel secure. The North emptied of its Muslims in 1990 shows exactly where the other road leads. A homeland cannot be just if its justice depends on keeping other people out.
What healing actually looks like
Healing is not a ceremony. It is not a speech, or two leaders shaking hands for the cameras.

It is land given back to the families who own it. Mothers finally told what happened to their sons. The dead of 2009 mourned openly, without anyone taking down names. Credible investigations into atrocities committed by every side. Equal treatment in every school and every government office. A hard, honest look at why soldiers still sit on civilian land in the North and East years after the fighting stopped. A war that has ended cannot justify a permanent shadow.
We were never born enemies

I don’t believe Sinhalese and Tamils were born to be enemies. Look at us. We eat rice and curry with our hands at the same kind of table. We lose sleep over the same cricket team. We stand in the same monsoon and curse the same potholes. For generations we have been manipulated by politicians who found that fear is easier to sell than trust, who turned our differences into weapons and handed them to us. We can stop taking them.

Our children already play together. That was never the hard part. The hard part is whole communities living without fear of one another. Parents who don’t wonder about the family next door. A Tamil woman who can speak her own language in a police station. A Muslim family returning to the North as neighbours, not as guests. A Sinhalese kid who can grieve for Black July without being called a traitor.

I want an island where you can be Tamil, Sinhalese, Muslim, Burgher, or anything else, and still be home. Where belonging is not a prize the majority hands down to the minority, and no one has to make anyone else smaller in order to stand tall.

A 24-year-old woman in Canada said her own name. The question was never whether she would call herself Sri Lankan. The question is whether Sri Lanka can become a country where a Tamil woman saying her name is heard as exactly that, a name, and nothing more.
More than two thousand years ago, a Tamil poet named Kaniyan Pungundranar gave the answer we are still trying to live up to:
Yaadhum oore, yaavarum kelir.
Every town is our town. Every person is our kin.
He wrote it before there was a Sri Lanka, before there was a war, before anyone thought to write a one-star review.
It is still the right answer.

8ce9d5b202e91471: KUALA LUMPUR: About 150 people gathered outside the Sogo shopping mall here today to take part in a protest against the alleged corporate mafia and the recent detention of two Mandiri activists.
The protesters started gathering at about 3pm as the crowd swelled to about 150 before they dispersed at about 5pm.

Among those present were former PKR MP Wong Chen, Muda president Amira Aisya Abdul Aziz, Parti Bangsa Malaysia (PBM) information chief Ronnie Liu, DAP Youth vice-chief Raja Ahmad Iskandar Fareez and activist Hishamuddin Rais.

The protesters listed three main demands for the government: a royal commission of inquiry to be formed over the corporate mafia allegations, an end to alleged double standards in law enforcement, and an end to the purported maltreatment of activists.

Addressing the crowd, Mandiri executive director Amir Hadi questioned the use of the Anti-Money Laundering, Anti-Terrorism Financing and Proceeds of Unlawful Activities Act 2001, or Amla, against activists.
This comes after he and Mandiri finance director Dobby Chew were detained for several days to assist in a money laundering probe.
Amir said the authorities should not be allowed to detain people and freeze their banks accounts before an offence was established.
“They can arrest us, put us in lock-up, charge us in court and even imprison us, but they will not be able to silence the voice of the people,” he said.
Amir said Mandiri will continue campaigning against corruption and pushing for those involved in the purported corporate mafia to be investigated and prosecuted.
Earlier this year, Bloomberg reported allegations that a network of businessmen and MACC officers used raids and investigations to pressure executives into selling shares in targeted companies.
The news network also reported allegations that then MACC chief Azam Baki had breached a government circular on civil servant shareholdings, which he denied.
This has led to calls for an RCI to be set up to probe the allegations, with DAP leaders also joining in.
Wong, who is now with Bersama, said an RCI is meant to establish the facts rather than presume anyone guilty.
“We are not saying they are already found guilty. We just want an RCI into Azam and the corporate mafia,” he said.
Muda secretary-general Ainie Haziqah Shafii urged young Malaysians to continue speaking out against the government when they disagreed with its actions, regardless of which coalition was in power.
“Just because Pakatan Harapan is in government, don't stop speaking out. If they are wrong, say they are wrong,” she said.

3d4d22cff10c9fd9: KAMPAR, Sept 27 — Terengganu Cycling Team (TSG) rider Muhammad Nur Aiman Rosli kicked off his Le Tour de Langkawi (LTdL) 2026 campaign brilliantly by securing the White Jersey as the Best Asian Rider after Stage 1 today.
The 27-year-old, who leads the chart after collecting points at two sprint zones in the 193-kilometre (km) race from Shah Alam to Kampar, admitted he initially planned a breakaway.
“I did plan a breakaway and managed to secure points at two sprint zones.

“For the third zone in Teluk Intan, I couldn’t keep up as I was too far behind the leading pack. Therefore, I had to ride smart to save energy for tomorrow’s race and focus on the next stage,” he told the media after the race.

Aiman Rosli finished the opening stage in a bunch finish, placing 70th out of 119 riders with a time of 4 hours, 6 minutes and 53 seconds (s). However, finishing third at the Ijok sprint zone and first in Kuala Selangor placed him at the top of the Asian category with 4:06:49s.

Aisan Racing Team’s Hijiri Oda is second in the Best Asian Rider chart with 4:06:53s, while Malaysia Pro Cycling’s Mohamad Izzat Hilmi Abdul Jalil, who emerged as the best local rider in the opening stage, is third with the same time.

Stage 2 tomorrow will see the peloton face a 145.6km challenge from Taiping to Gunung Jerai, featuring three sprint zones in Selama (km 41), Padang Serai and Aman Jaya, as well as two climb zones in Selama (km 53.6) and Gunung Jerai.
The climb up Gunung Jerai is a special highlight, as it is featured in the prestigious race calendar for the first time since its introduction in 1996.
Aware of the gruelling hilly route tomorrow, the seven-time consecutive national champion, who is the team’s sprint specialist, stressed the need to manage his energy carefully.
“I have to ‘save my legs’ because tomorrow’s stage features quite steep climbs. It is a blessing to wear the Best Asian Rider jersey. For tomorrow, we will have a different plan,” he said.

Meanwhile, Aiman expressed hope that teammate Kee Zhe Yie, currently second in the King of the Mountains chart behind Wheeltop Rotor Chengdu Team’s Petr Rikunov, could maintain his excellent momentum.
“I told Zhe Yie to try his best for the team. Hopefully, he can do something for the team and himself,” he added. — Bernama

10b1ebb068692932: KUALA LUMPUR, Sept 27 — Former minister in the Prime Minister’s Department (Federal Territories) Datuk Seri Dr Zaliha Mustafa denied allegations that she had attended, officiated, or been involved in any groundbreaking ceremonies for new settlements for Myanmar refugees.
She emphasised that the allegations circulating on social media are false and malicious, in addition to linking a photograph of her with an individual to something that never happened.
“I do not personally know the individual in question and do not have any relationship or dealings, whether official or unofficial, with him,” she said in a Facebook post today.

Dr Zaliha explained that based on the review, the circulated photo is believed to have been taken at the Asean Sustainable Urbanisation Forum (ASUF), Asean Governors and Mayors Forum (AGMF), and Meeting of Governors and Mayors of Asean Capitals (MGMAC) 2025 in the capital city on August 12, 2025.

According to her, she was invited to deliver a special address and subsequently attend the Joint Launch Ceremony for the programme, which was officiated by Deputy Prime Minister Datuk Seri Fadillah Yusof.
“The programme is open to the public to register as participants. Therefore, I certainly do not know the identity of every individual who attended.
“A photo with a participant does not mean I know the person, have a relationship with him, invited him personally, or support his views or actions,” she said.

The Sekijang Member of Parliament said she would report the matter to the Malaysian Communications and Multimedia Commission (MCMC) regarding the dissemination of the post for review and appropriate action according to the law.

Meanwhile, Dr Zaliha said the allegation that she supported or facilitated the resettlement of new Myanmar refugees was also inconsistent with the record of actions she took while leading the Federal Territories Department.

She said that among the measures implemented was the establishment of the KL Strike Force as an integrated enforcement mechanism to address issues of security and public order, particularly in the capital, including the issue of the influx of foreign nationals and the illegal settlement of Myanmar refugees.

“In fact, the first operation of the KL Strike Force was to raid the illegal settlement of Myanmar refugees in Bandar Baru Sentul. Through KL Strike Force, I emphasised that action should be taken against illegal settlements and structures, unlicensed businesses, and foreign activities without proper authorisation,” she also said.
Therefore, she urged all parties not to take a single photo out of context to build a narrative that is not based on facts. — Bernama
fb1b0d8b82207dd7: KOTA BHARU, Sept 27 — The General Operations Force (GOF) seized 15,000 robusta coffee seedlings and a lorry with a total value of RM1 million during a roadblock at Lalang Pepuyu, Tanah Merah, last night.
GOF Southeast Brigade commander SAC Ahmad Radzi Hussain said a 27-year-old man who was driving the lorry was detained during the operation at 11.30pm.
“An inspection of the lorry’s cargo compartment uncovered 15,000 robusta coffee seedlings believed to have been smuggled from Thailand.
“The total value of the seizure was estimated at RM1 million, comprising the lorry worth RM250,000 and the coffee seedlings worth RM750,000,” he said in a statement today.
He said preliminary investigation found that the man had collected the seedlings from an illegal jetty in the Lalang Pepuyu area to deliver them to a nursery in Johor for RM300 per delivery.
“All the seedlings were handed over to the Kota Bharu Agriculture Department for further action as they are suspected of containing pests,” he said.
Ahmad Radzi said the seedlings would be inspected before being disposed of, while a compound could be issued if the offence involving pests was confirmed.
The case is being investigated under the Plant Quarantine Act 1976 (Act 167), he added. — Bernama

6b2a41edaaa7a802: PETALING JAYA: The road transport department (JPJ) says it will continue its enforcement on luxury vehicles for various offences, after the success of its operations over the past 16 months.

This was revealed by JPJ senior director of enforcement Kifli Ma Hassan who said a total of 3,790 luxury vehicles worth an estimated RM550 million were seized by the department under Op Luxury since June 2025, Bernama reported.
He said 785 vehicles were seized between June and December 2025, while another 3,005 were seized between January and Sept 26, this year.
He said Negeri Sembilan recorded the highest number of seizures with 469 vehicles, followed by Selangor (410), Kuala Lumpur (382), Johor (367) and Penang (357).
“Some luxury vehicle owners said they were reluctant to go to JPJ offices to renew their road tax because they had been blacklisted for previous offences.

“What is puzzling is that lower-income groups can come forward to renew their road tax, while owners of luxury vehicles from the T20 group give various reasons for not doing so, resulting in their vehicles being seized,” he told a press conference at the JPJ office in Kota Bharu, Kelantan today.
According to Kifli, JPJ found that an estimated 20% of the luxury vehicle owners were cosmetic entrepreneurs, influencers and businesspeople.
He said JPJ would continue Op Luxury to ensure that all road users comply with the law, regardless of the price or type of vehicle, or the status of its owner.
“Being able to afford a luxury vehicle comes with the responsibility to comply with the law.

"Owners and drivers are responsible for ensuring that all vehicle and driving documents remain valid, and that their vehicles meet all requirements before being driven on the road,” he was quoted as saying.
Last December, it was reported that the luxury car brands seized by JPJ included Lamborghini, Aston Martin, Ferrari, and Rolls-Royce.
5a1e91e947ab69b4: LUCKNOW: Heavy rain triggered floods and landslides in the northern Indian state of Uttar Pradesh, killing at least 56 people over the past three days, a government disaster agency said on Sunday.
Uttar Pradesh, India's most populous state with more than 240 million people, is frequently battered by rain and thunderstorms during the annual monsoon season from June to September.
The latest deaths were reported during a spell of "exceptionally heavy rain that has affected much of Uttar Pradesh", the Relief Commissioner's office said in a statement.
More than 1,000 houses were damaged after "a depression over the Bay of Bengal moved inland and intensified rainfall across the region", it said.

India's weather office has warned in recent years of an increase in extreme weather events, including intense thunderstorms and lightning, which experts link to rising temperatures and changing climate patterns.
The statement said the state recorded 66.5 millimetres of rain between Friday and Sunday, compared to the season average of 7.6 millimetres.

72079cb36e016fe3: PORTADOWN, Sept 27 — UK Prime Minister Andy Burnam urged “calm” today as thousands of people gathered in a Northern Irish town seeking to halt a contentious pro-British Protestant march from passing through a mainly Catholic and nationalist area for the first time in 28 years.
The tensions spiked after a court in the early hours of today cleared the march by the Orange Order to go ahead.

The Parades Commission, Northern Ireland’s independent body regulating contentious processions, had authorised 35 Orangemen to march silently along Garvaghy Road in Portadown, without bands or supporters from 8am (0700 GMT/3pm Malaysian time) today.
Burnham appealed for “calm on all sides”, adding in an interview with BBC television that that “big gains” had been made in Northern Ireland “and we don’t want to see things go backwards”.

Northern Ireland was blighted for three decades by conflict between largely Catholic, pro-Irish republicans and Protestant, pro-UK unionists, and the Garvaghy Road became a major flashpoint during the late 1990s.
About 2,000 people walked early today in the Garvaghy Road area of Portadown, 25 miles southwest of Belfast, in a counter-protest seeking to prevent the Orange march.
There was a heavy security presence, and police held up the Orange Order rally inside a church hall, an AFP correspondent saw.
Northern Ireland First Minister Michelle O’Neill, of the Irish republican Sinn Fein party, condemned the late-night court ruling allowing the march to go ahead.
“Our message tonight is clear. There is no going back. Not tomorrow. Not ever,” said O’Neill.
She said she supported “the right of the Garvaghy Road residents to protest against this unwanted sectarian march”.

Sinn Fein President Mary Lou McDonald told reporters as she walked with the counter-protesters that the “residents and community have come out to defend their right to live free from sectarian harassment”.

Since the 1998 Good Friday peace accords ending the so-called Troubles in Northern Ireland “there has been lots of progress... it has been transformational. People’s lives have been changed fundamentally,” she said, adding “we are not going back”.
The procession had survived a series of last-minute legal challenges.
A Belfast High Court judge temporarily blocked it yesterday, warning that the long-running dispute could escalate across Northern Ireland and urging the parties to “step back from the abyss”.
But shortly before midnight, a three-judge Court of Appeal panel overturned the injunction, ruling that the judge had “erred in law”.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->

Stickers cover a road sign as a crowd of protesters gather to block the Garvaghy Road in Portadown, Northern Ireland in the morning of September 27, 2026, to prevent a parade of marchers from the Orange Order using the route through the mainly nationalist area of the town. — AFP pic
‘Nothing to fear’
The substantive legal challenge was returned to the High Court, but the appeal decision left the procession free to begin at 8am (0700 GMT) today.
Carla Lockhart, a local MP from the pro-British Democratic Unionist Party, called the appeal overturn “seismic” and said residents had nothing to fear.
“Thirty-five men walking down a road silently with no bands in an orderly fashion; there is nothing to fear,” she said.
The confrontation, known as the Drumcree dispute after the church attended by the marchers, became a major flashpoint during the late 1990s.
Attempts to force the parade through, or prevent it from proceeding, repeatedly triggered serious disorder.
The Parades Commission was established in 1998, the year the Good Friday Agreement largely ended three decades of conflict over British rule known as the Troubles.
It barred the Order from completing the route that year and has consistently rejected subsequent applications.
The issue was revived in August when the High Court quashed the commission’s latest restriction because of procedural failings, without ruling that the Order had a right to march along Garvaghy Road.
The Order then submitted a fresh application, leading to Friday’s decision permitting the restricted procession.

The Orange Order is an pro-British organisation that takes its name from William of Orange, the Protestant Dutchman who seized the English, Scottish and Ireland throne from Catholic King James II in 1689. — AFP
914bb2017c706e9d: Thirty years after Apple abandoned Copland, its doomed attempt to create a modern Mac operating system, a new emulator lets you try the final developer build in your browser. Copland was intended to replace Apple's System 7 with a PowerPC-native operating system built around a microkernel, protected memory, and preemptive multitasking for system services. Three unfinished developer builds – D7E1, D9, and D11E4 – are publicly known. Relatively few people outside Apple's developer community in the mid-1990s ever had the opportunity to use them. Now you can boot Apple Copland D11E4 in your browser and explore the unstable prerelease OS without installing anything. Developer Michael Steil, also known as Mist, made it possible with an experimental fork of the DingusPPC Power Mac emulator. Steil says the 11 patches that enable DingusPPC to boot Copland were written with AI assistance. The upstream project does not accept AI-assisted patches, so the fixes would have to be rewritten before they could be incorporated. Don't expect miracles. The emulator runs D11E4, the final build Apple distributed to developers, dating from June 1996. It remains very much unfinished: if the emulated system hits an assertion, it drops into a debugger and asks the user to continue manually. Apple CEO Gil Amelio had demonstrated Copland at the company's 1995 Worldwide Developers Conference, but the project never approached the stability required for release. Much of Copland existed as plans and documentation rather than finished code. In 2009, Steil assembled an extensive archive of that material in Apple Copland Reference Documentation. There was also a planned successor to Copland, codenamed Gershwin, but it remained nothing more than a plan. The modern Gershwin desktop we covered a year ago is a nod to that nonexistent OS. Anyone familiar with the classic Mac OS of the late 1990s will recognize parts of Copland, and for good reason. Copland overran so badly that Amelio recruited the late Ellen Hancock from IBM as Apple's chief technology officer and tasked her with getting the project back on track. After reviewing its progress, she instead recommended cancelling it and acquiring an operating system elsewhere. Apple considered several alternatives, including acquiring Be for BeOS and working with Sun on a system based on Solaris. It ultimately bought NeXT, bringing Steve Jobs back to the company along with NeXTSTEP. Hancock was later sidelined under Jobs and resigned in 1997. Apple acquired NeXT at the end of 1996, just months after cancelling Copland. The first developer release of its NeXTSTEP-based successor, Rhapsody, followed in 1997 – continuing the musical codenames, if not the code. Rhapsody evolved into Mac OS X Server 1.0 in 1999 and the consumer release of Mac OS X 10.0 in 2001. Replacing the Mac OS architecture took years. While that work continued, Apple folded some of Copland's more mature components into updates to its existing operating system. Mac OS 8, released in 1997, gained Copland's Platinum interface and a PowerPC-native, multithreaded Finder. Its Appearance control panel supported themes, although Apple shipped only Platinum. Renaming what had been planned as Mac OS 7.7 also helped Apple end the clone program, whose licensing agreements covered System 7. Mac OS 8.1 followed in 1998 with HFS+, Apple's new format for larger disks. Later that year, Mac OS 8.5 became the first PowerPC-only release. Further pieces of Copland's work appeared across Mac OS 8 and 9, allowing Apple to improve the old platform while Mac OS X was being prepared. When Apple bought NeXT, NeXTSTEP already ran on Motorola 680x0, Intel x86, Sun SPARC and HP PA-RISC processors. That portable foundation later helped Apple move the Mac to Intel, while OS X became the basis for the operating systems used by the iPhone and iPad. Apple's future might have looked very different had Copland succeeded. Now it's easier than ever to see why it didn't. ®
d704124e37716f21: NAGOYA, Sept 27 — National squash queen S. Sivasangari lived up to expectations by defending her Asian Games women’s singles gold medal after defeating India’s Anahat Singh 11-4, 11-4, 11-7 in the Aichi-Nagoya 2026 final today.
The victory at the Nagoya Kinjofuto Arena saw Sivasangari retain her Hangzhou 2022 title, and secured her a berth at the Los Angeles 2028 Olympic Games (LA28).
The Kedah-born player delivered a composed performance to complete a stellar campaign, handing the national contingent its sixth gold medal.
Her win continued the national squash team’s excellent run at the Games, following Ng Eain Yow’s successful title defence in the men’s singles earlier in the day.
The victory also helped Malaysia reach its six-gold medal target for the Games. — Bernama
928f9fbf45c75243: ALOR GAJAH, Sept 27 — Two men, aged 57 and 38, were found dead in separate incidents in Alor Gajah today.
Alor Gajah district police chief Supt Ahmad Abu Bakar said police received a report regarding the discovery of a 57-year-old man at 11.30am in an abandoned shophouse in Cherana Putih, Taboh Naning.
He said the body believed to have been dead for two days was discovered by a member of the public in the area.
“A preliminary examination of the body revealed no signs of foul play, and the victim is believed to have been in the area without his family’s knowledge,” he told reporters here today.
In a related development, Ahmad said the second case involved a 38-year-old man found dead in an apartment unit in Simpang Ampat at approximately noon.
He said the victim was a factory worker who lived alone, was discovered by his fiancée after failing to answer phone calls since the previous night.
The fiancée entered the home through a window and found the victim unconscious before calling an ambulance.
“No signs of break-in or foul play were detected in either incident, and the cases have been classified as sudden death (SDR).
“Both bodies have been taken to Alor Gajah Hospital for post-mortem to determine the exact cause of death,” he said. — Bernama
020783b14d1b002c: NAGOYA, Sept 27 — Asian Games organisers in Japan said today they had been caught off guard by complaints about some of the accommodation and promised athletes coming for the final week a more comfortable stay.
In a break from previous Games, organisers in Aichi-Nagoya did not construct a traditional athletes’ village in order to save money.
Instead, the more than 17,000 athletes and officials — a greater number than the Olympics — are staying in hotels, temporary wooden units and on a cruise ship.
Some teams have complained about the shipping container-style units, saying the rooms are cramped and the beds too short.
Yuta Matsuo, deputy director of athletes’ accommodation, said there had been “issues that went beyond what we expected”.
“But we believe that we have responded appropriately so that delays in addressing them did not cause major inconvenience for the athletes or make it difficult to run the competitions,” he said.
“We will continue to listen closely to athletes’ needs and requests and address them going forward.”
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
Officials walks past temporary container huts during a press tour of the athletes’ village during the 2026 Asian Games at the Garden Pier in Nagoya September 27, 2026. — AFP pic
South Korean officials said that the container hut rooms were the “worst ever”, with beds too small for their country’s basketball team.
Games officials invited the media in today to see for themselves.
There are 200 huts, which will house a total of 2,000 athletes over the duration of the Games, with three or four athletes in each unit.
Each hut has a floor area of 35 square metres and measure 230cm from floor to ceiling.
Toilets are equipped for athletes staying for the Asian Para Games, and beds are separated by curtains.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
This photo shows a room in a temporary container hut during a press tour of the athletes’ village during the 2026 Asian Games at the Garden Pier in Nagoya September 27, 2026. — AFP pic
The interior walls of the huts are bare wood, and although there is a kitchen sink, there is no equipment for cooking.
A strong smell of wood is noticeable.
Athletes eat in a large communal dining room, with a shop, medical centre, fitness centre and a space to interact with other athletes on the site.
IOC president Kirsty Coventry has called the container units “beautiful” but conceded they were “a little tighter” than similar accommodation at the Milan-Cortina Winter Olympics.
Matsuo said organisers expected more issues to arise and vowed to respond appropriately.
“Athletes’ needs and requests differ greatly according to their cultural background and customs,” he said.
“When problems occur, our focus has been on how quickly we can respond, and how we can respond at any time.” — AFP
5257d9aa0dc71f0b: GENEVA: The Swiss voted Sunday on a much-debated proposal to tighten their country's cherished neutrality, with polls indicating most would reject the initiative championed by the hard-right and dubbed "pro-Russian" by opponents.
Polling stations opened on Sunday morning for in-person voting on those and other topics as part of Switzerland's direct democracy system, although most people vote in advance by post.
The Swiss widely embrace their neutrality, but an initiative to enshrine a strict definition into the constitution has exposed deep disagreement over what that neutrality entails.
Switzerland's traditional position is one of armed neutrality, but Russia's war in Ukraine reopened questions over its non-engagement in foreign conflicts.

Concerned over Bern's decision to back the EU's economic pressure on Russia, the pro-sovereignty Pro Switzerland organisation collected enough signatures to trigger a referendum under the country's direct democracy system on better anchoring neutrality in its constitution.
The proposal has been roundly rejected by nearly the entire political establishment, with opinion polls indicating most voters will do the same.
Moscow, which has slammed Switzerland for joining the EU sanctions and accused Bern of abandoning its neutrality, has meanwhile praised the initiative - dubbed "pro-Russian" by some opponents.
The proposal calls for the constitution to guarantee that Swiss neutrality is "armed and perpetual".

It would prevent Switzerland, whose neutrality dates back to 1516 and has been internationally recognised since 1815, from establishing closer ties with Nato and would rule out any military alliance except if the country were attacked.
It would prohibit imposing sanctions unless called for by the UN.
'Perpetual armed neutrality'
All sides in the debate argue that they want to maintain Switzerland's neutrality.
Both the Swiss government and parliament have rejected the proposal, arguing it is too dogmatic and would limit the country's room for manoeuvre at a time of soaring geopolitical tensions.
"Neutrality has always been applied with a degree of flexibility," Swiss foreign minister Ignazio Cassis said during a recent televised debate.
While Switzerland had no plans to lift a ban on selling arms to countries in conflict, including to Ukraine, he stressed that "neutrality does not mean indifference".
The country, he said, would "not look away when we see violations of the very international rules that allow us to live in peace".
Nearly all major political parties have also turned their nose up at the initiative, with the exception of the hard-right Swiss People's Party (SVP), the country's largest party.
"Our goal is to foster peace, diplomacy and dialogue," SVP vice-president Celine Amaudruz said during a televised debate.
"To achieve that, we must maintain credibility through perpetual armed neutrality," she insisted.
While initial opinion polls had indicated that the vote might be tight, the final two surveys suggested a clear majority of voters - well above 60%- would reject the initiative.

Polls also suggested voters would reject the other national initiative on Sunday's ballot, put forward by a non-partisan citizens' movement and calling for the country to raise its food self-sufficiency rate to 70%, up from 42% in 2024.
The government has warned that the target would be difficult, if not impossible, to reach, while most major parties also reject it as unrealistic.
Polling stations will close at 12pm at the latest.
e6768316f1ac5209: PETALING JAYA: The Islamic development department (Jakim) has issued deputy religious affairs minister Marhamah Rosli with an advisory after content she published in 2019 was linked to New Age movements.
Jakim director-general Sirajuddin Suhaimee said this involved content and methods Marhamah previously used which prompted questions from the public.
Sirajuddin said Marhamah had been called in to explain the matter, with the meeting joined by the federal territories mufti, a Jakim panel of experts, and other authorities.
“Following the meeting, several reprimands, advisories and guidelines were given, including over the content of programmes that had been carried out and the approaches used,” he said in a statement.

He said this was to ensure any content that could cause confusion to Muslims about fundamental Islamic beliefs was corrected, adding that programmes must always be based on recognised Islamic disciplines.
The controversy was partly sparked by a recirculated screenshot of a Facebook post published by Marhamah in September 2019.
The deputy minister has strongly denied claims she promoted New Age teachings, witchcraft, magic, or the use of charms.
On Sept 18, her office gave those spreading the allegations 24 hours to remove the claims and issue a public apology, failing which legal action could be considered.
d2dfe33bda6046d1: Big AI has a problem. Its companies must ingest other people’s work. You know, books, news stories, photographs, code, websites, that one original meme you came up with, and practically everything else on the internet to train its large language models (LLMs). We all know that. We also know that AI companies hate paying for any of it, obeying the licenses attached to it, or, God forbid, sharing their revenue with the companies and people who created the work in the first place. Recently, Big AI's default way of doing business: "Take it now, argue about legality later," has become more in your face than ever. Look, for example, at the copyright fight between The New York Times and OpenAI and Microsoft. According to 404 Media’s reporting on recently unsealed court documents - arguments from the plaintiffs that the court has not yet ruled on - Microsoft allegedly knew what it was doing when it was importing the internet willy-nilly. Microsoft's Director of Applied Science, Dr. Brent Hecht, was quoted in the news plaintiffs' 92-page combined brief as saying: the case was about “an astonishing theft of unprecedented proportions." Indeed, it was possibly the “largest theft of labor in human history,” he was quoted as saying in the summary judgment brief from the journalists' lawyers [PDF].This, mind you, wasn't a comment by a member of the press; it was from a senior Microsoft staffer. Hecht wasn't the only one at Microsoft who commented. In an internal Microsoft policy document also quoted in the court papers, the authors admitted generative AI could “significantly disrupt the employment of the very people who generated the data on which the foundation model was trained [because] LLMs are a product that destroys its supply chain.” That, in turn, leads to model collapse. Ironically, AI is killing the content-creator goose that lays the gold eggs of worthwhile content. Judge Sidney H. Stein of the US District Court for the Southern District of New York has not yet issued a decision on the case. OpenAI and Microsoft are actively disputing the plaintiffs' allegations under a "fair use" defense. They contend that using public articles and books to train large language models helps push forward public knowledge, and isn't acting as a "unlawful economic market substitute". But the statements the documents cites are real. Big AI knows it needs the content. Some of the companies concerned don't give a damn; money now, worry later is their motto. Those who can look past the revenue numbers are well aware they're engaged in what Microsoft itself called a “doom loop” of AI content strategy in those unsealed court documents. Will that stop them? Nah. According to the filing [PDF], which refers to sworn deposition testimony of OpenAI’s own corporate representative, it also testified that its LLMs were happy to vacuum up other people's work even when a paywall nominally protected it. Its rep was quoted as saying they were unaware of “any effort to detect paywall content in its training datasets” or “to remove paywall content from its training datasets.” When OpenAI cofounder Greg Brockman was told OpenAI could hack its way through the firewall, he responded, “ah, nice.” Whether or not these statements are found to be reflective of a wider attitude, similar attitudes prevail amongst Big AI. Such policies could eventually come back and bite the LLM makers; it's already affecting the market for journalism, fiction writing, graphics creation, anything that demands humans actually get paid for producing original work. But Big AI just doesn't want to pay for it. That's not a side effect. It's the business model. Joe User couldn't care less. They just want a quick answer that sounds right. Some of them couldn't care less about getting the right answers. As for looking deeper to see if the information they're regurgitating is accurate, forget about it! As an OpenAI software engineer put it: “No matter how prominently we show the links, users won’t click.” Well, I click. That's a big reason why Perplexity is my AI of choice. It's not that it gives a more reliable answer. No, it's that, unlike most LLMs, Perplexity provides sources and links, and I check them before accepting what it tells me. But then I'm a journalist whose degrees are in history, where my professors drummed into me that you always - always - look at the primary sources. Big AI takes the same approach with its code generators. The US Ninth Circuit recently handed GitHub, Microsoft, and OpenAI a narrow win in the Doe v. GitHub lawsuit. The court ruled that the plaintiffs hadn't established a claim under one particular provision of the Digital Millennium Copyright Act (DMCA), which concerns the removal or alteration of copyright-management information (CMI). In short, the court said that generating new code without including CMI is not necessarily the same thing as removing or altering copyright information from an existing work. Judge Eric Miller wrote: “One who creates a new work and fails to include CMI cannot be said to have ‘removed’ or ‘altered’ anything.” This ruling didn't establish that GitHub Copilot or any other coding model may train on every open source project without restriction. It didn't determine that copying source code into a training set is always fair use. It did not decide that generated code cannot infringe copyright. And it certainly did not repeal the GPL, Apache, BSD, MIT, or any other open-source license. After all, open source isn't a synonym for “do whatever you want with it.” It just seems that way when AI gets its hands on open source code. That's the problem with AI-generated code. A programmer who receives a Copilot suggestion is very unlikely to check whether the GPL covers the code, or whether Apache covers the snippet from a library. The developer certainly can't tell which license terms may apply to the code that just popped up from Opus 5.5 or GPT 6. As the guy from OpenAI said, people don't click the links, and in AI-enabled programming pipelines, they don't even have the links anyway. An open source-savvy attorney friend of mine has a bigger worry than this narrow decision. He told me that what gives him "pause is a broader trend. There are multiple cases where parties are litigating open source licenses as contracts rather than as the IP / copyright licenses they were written to be. Contract theories let a plaintiff sidestep the questions copyright forces you to answer. 'Do you own the work? Is it protectable expression? Was it actually copied?'" He added: "Those questions are the foundation on which licenses are built. Open source licenses are grants of permission to use someone's intellectual property. If a case can't show that any intellectual property was owned or infringed, it's fair to ask whether enforcing the license as a bare contract supports open source licensing or quietly turns it into something else." With AI in the mix, this issue will eventually become one of those nasty IP matters developers hate, businesses want to avoid, but that courts must settle with expensive lawyers whose hourly rates worry even AI millionaires. After all, IP uncertainty isn't a minor paperwork issue. It is a supply-chain security and compliance problem. If you use AI-generated code, you may be importing unknown legal obligations into your software. If you are an open-source developer, your work may be used to improve a proprietary service that returns code without provenance, attribution, or meaningful reciprocity. And if you are a customer, you may be relying on software whose origins no one can fully explain. The Ninth Circuit ruling didn't solve any of that. We're in for a lot more open source litigation that will make SCO vs. the known Linux universe look like a kerfuffle over a parking ticket. Then there is the latest wrinkle: A federal antitrust lawsuit against Anthropic, OpenAI, SpaceXAI, and Google. The plaintiffs allege the companies coordinated to slow the development of advanced AI systems. The lawsuit points to public statements from AI leaders all calling for coordination to “pace” frontier AI development over a single weekend. Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei has argued for industry-wide coordination to slow frontier development. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, Google DeepMind co-founder Demis Hassabis, and Elon Musk have also publicly expressed versions of the view that powerful AI systems need controls and careful deployment. On its face, that sounds sensible. AI safety is a real issue. Anyone who says otherwise has not been paying attention. But there's a huge difference between all big AI players agreeing among themselves on how quickly a market should develop. This looks like an awful lot like competitors deciding who gets to compete, what they get to build, and when they may build it. The Big AI companies all look like good guys while simultaneously strangling their smaller competitors. To mere mortals, this may sound like an open-and-shut case. It's not. Antitrust law requires evidence of an agreement and actual harm to competition; executives making similar public comments is not enough. The plaintiffs will need considerably more than quotes about AI safety or responsible development to win. Besides, if they do win, so what? What recently looked like huge antitrust wins has had its teeth pulled when it came to actually punishing the likes of Google and its ad business, or its earlier "lose the case, win the settlement" with Google Search. Do you see the pattern here? Big AI has effectively argued that copyright law, open source licenses, and competition rules shouldn't slow them down. When creators object, they are told that training is fair use. When developers object, they are told that generated code is new code. When competitors object, they are told security requires the largest companies to coordinate. Funny how the answer always seems to leave Big AI with the data, the market, and the money, isn't it? The central issue isn't whether AI should be allowed to develop. It will develop. The issue is whether the companies building it should be allowed to treat everyone else’s work as a free raw-material supply, then use the resulting products to take away the creators’ traffic, revenue, and bargaining power. Unless we stop Big AI now from this land grab with GPUs, only a handful of trillionaires will really benefit from AI, with the rest of us becoming serfs in a 21st-century post-technology feudal system. ®
